Basic Income is not welfare. Although some politicians and economists have considered it in the context of a more cost-effective alternative to welfare systems, it has an entirely different premise. Basic Income is premised on a Georgist economics principle of a just individual dividend on the exploitation and development of a nation's resources and publically funded infrastructure. It is intended to be granted to every citizen, universally and unconditionally, without any kind of 'means testing' which incurs undue costs to a welfare system. Thus it is often called a Universal/Unconditional Basic Income--UBI. We, as a society, own the natural resources of the nation and resources developed with public money; ie roads, municipal utilities building with tax money, etc. These resources are the ultimate source of all domestic product. When a commercial interest utilizes these resources, we the people are justly owed interest on that use of the societal commons just as if we were shareholders of a corporation. In Georgist theory it is unjust to tax income but just to tax property as rent or interest on the use of the resource commons. Government taxes the commercial users of national resources then, in theory, uses this for the benefit of the collective society. Basic Income's essential suggestion is that this is undemocratic. It should be up to society individually as to what to do with this dividend, and so it is the state's obligation to disburse this dividend to the entire society and let them use it as they see fit.

Basic Income is a very old idea. It was proposed even by the US's founding fathers. But it has always been controversial because, at its root, is this suggestion that you cannot own anything you didn't actually make/produce yourself. All 'real' property is owned by society as a commons. And so all such property can only be rented from the commons (with interest owed to society), and those rights of use revoked as the society democratically sees fit. And there's also the issue of the individual rights of states to their resources as opposed to the larger nation. This is seen as a just, democratic, alternative to the traditional theory of property that ownership of everything originates in a god who, in turn, grants property to his anointed representatives (kings), who then grant it to a nobility in exchange for service/loyalty (cash loans...) to the crown, who then grant, sell, or rent it out as they see fit.

Beyond the theory comes the question of where the money for a basic income comes from and how it gets disbursed to society. Typically, it's suggested as a cut out of the tax income of a nation. But there have been other more interesting ideas. Economist Louis Kelso, who worked with Buckminster Fuller and is most well known for his invention of the Employee Stock Ownership Program, proposed the creation of a Capital Homesteading Act as part of what he dubbed a "just third way" of economics. Another system neither Capitalist nor Socialist. The CHA was intended to create a kind of national mutual fund investing in all publicly financed corporations. A key idea for Kelso was that the key to economic justice in society was direct ownership of the means of production. And so he was always interested in ways of expanding the individual public ownership of the national GDP, hence the idea of the ESOP, its companion the CSOP (consumer stock ownership program--if you use a lot of something--like gasoline and electricity--you should earn interest in the companies that produce it), and the Community Investment Corporation or Land-Home Bank. That's not always practical in a direct sense, so the next best thing was to use the conventional mechanisms of community ownership in the finance industry toward that end. And so Kelso's UBI was, basically, a stock dividend on every company in the nation.

But disbursing Basic Income is tricky because, frankly, the business world mostly consists of assholes. Many economists fear the benefits of a UBI mailed out like a check on a regular date will disappear in cyclic spikes of price gouging or an escalation in inflation. It's a common problem in communities of the poor. The store owners all know exactly when the welfare checks get mailed out and, magically, all the prices in shops in those areas go up that week. The poor always pay more. So many economists think we need to devise ways of 'stealthing' the UBI into the economy to circumvent the compulsive asshattery.

Basic Income also doesn't need to exist as cash. Futurists today often talk about ubiquitous automated production, moneyless cultures, and people simply taking what they want off of store shelves. People wonder how that can possibly work. Well, in the context of that technology there is the potential to create an 'Integral Basic Income' that's coded into the production networks as a function of quantitative analysis on demand. Really, all money is for is a metric of the flow of value and demand. In an automated economic system, you don't need such abstractions. You can not only measure demand directly but also predict it with great accuracy through the same quantitative analysis used in commodities trading. Money is redundant. So if you can 'digitally' understand and can predict what society needs with sufficient depth and accuracy, you just code it into the automated networked resource distribution and people just take whatever they need, 'free within reason'. The so-called Star Trek Economics. That's an Integral Basic Income.

Experiments like what Y-Combinator are proposing are popping up all over the world. There's one called MyBasicIncome that works kind of like a lottery. Participants pledge a little money every month to provide a Basic Income for one or a few randomly selected members for a year. These aren't real Basic Incomes because they're not linked to any GDP or a societal commons. They really just human behavior experiments. About seeing what people do with a Basic Income when they have it. And this is because, to a lot of people, this is such a new and alien concept they suspect it must be doomed by human behavior. No matter how many times psychologists disprove the 'conventional wisdom' that we're all compulsively selfish pigs who would be like kids locked in a candy store if given 'free money', the Racists, the Suits, and the Fudds still want this proven over and over again.

50 years from now, I think it will seem ridiculous that we used fear of not being able to eat as a way to motivate people.

Angus Deaton's book "The Great Escape: Health, Wealth, and the Origins of Inequality" effectively details why FOOD is not the issue. When "poverty" benchmarks were explored earlier in the 20th century, food costs made up a large percentage of household budgets, even in the "developed" nations. So having no better ideas, and as it seemed logical, government agencies used food pricing benchmarks to set the levels of aid necessary. When they ran the numbers the calculations "seemed" correct and felt correct to those making the assumptions. However that has not been the case since the 1970's. Now, it is housing that makes up the greatest expense -- in some areas it is 50% of people's take-home pay, while food costs are trivial by comparison.

In fact one of the big problems Deaton explores is how poverty-line calculations, calculations for the "minimum wage" and many other markers for economic "welfare" are still archaicly based off of food prices; distorting all sorts of calculations in a world where shelter, healthcare, education and transportation have taken center stage in terms of costs.
I think it's great that research is being done, but I'm very skeptical of it working. I'm also a bit worried about the researchers being biased.
